**The Theory of the Leisure Class**
Veblen's most famous book (1899), a satirical analysis of how the wealthy show their status through wasteful spending and conspicuous leisure. It traces the leisure class back to "barbarian" and "predatory" stages of culture. Veblen was a Norwegian-American economist and a founder of institutional economics.

**Conspicuous consumption**
The term Veblen coined in The Theory of the Leisure Class for spending on luxury goods and services mainly to show off wealth and social standing rather than for their usefulness. It is the most common giveaway for him.

**Veblen goods**
Luxury goods named for him, for which demand rises as the price rises, because a high price makes them more prestigious. They are a famous exception to the law of demand.

**Pecuniary emulation**
Veblen's term, from an early chapter of The Theory of the Leisure Class, for the competition in which people imitate the consumption of those above them in order to gain status and respect.

**"The Belief in Luck"**
A chapter of The Theory of the Leisure Class arguing that the human tendency to gamble comes from belief in luck, a holdover of "predatory culture." Veblen similarly treated the competitive, social Darwinist outlook as a survival of prehistoric barbarism.

**The Engineers and the Price System**
Veblen's 1921 book contrasting efficient industrial production run by engineers with businessmen's focus on profit, which he thought led them to restrict output. It proposed that technical experts run the economy and influenced the later technocracy movement.

**The Theory of Business Enterprise**
Veblen's 1904 book on the conflict between "industry" (making goods) and "business" (making money). It analyzes the credit economy and links stock market values of companies to investment, an idea seen as anticipating Tobin's q.

**Imperial Germany and the Industrial Revolution**
Veblen's 1915 book arguing that Germany, a late industrializer under an authoritarian dynastic state, could use modern technology more effectively than democratic Britain and France, which were held back by older business habits and institutions.

**Absentee Ownership**
Veblen's 1923 book, in full Absentee Ownership and Business Enterprise in Recent Times, on American business between World War I and the Great Depression. It criticizes owners who profit from enterprises they do not directly run.

**"Why Is Economics Not an Evolutionary Science?"**
Veblen's 1898 essay criticizing classical economics as not "up to date." He argued that economics should be an evolutionary theory of cumulative cultural and institutional growth, in the spirit of Darwin.

**"The Place of Science in Modern Civilization"**
Veblen's essay arguing that a matter-of-fact scientific outlook is the defining characteristic of modern Western civilization. It is also the title of a later collection of his essays.

**"The Beginnings of Ownership" and "The Barbarian Status of Women"**
Two essays Veblen published in the American Journal of Sociology around 1898–1899. They trace private property and patriarchy back to the seizure of women as trophies in early "barbarian" society.

**"Devout Observance"**
A chapter of The Theory of the Leisure Class on religion, which presents religious ritual and church spending as forms of conspicuous waste and vicarious leisure.

**Silver spoons and pecuniary canons of taste**
In The Theory of the Leisure Class, Veblen argues that people admire costly handmade silverware over equally useful cheap spoons because its expense signals status, so that beauty becomes confused with costliness.
